paragraphs: “He talks quite coherently,” thought Ivan, “mumbling aside. Where’s this impairment of his faculties that Herzenstube spoke of?”
“You’re being sly with me, damn you!” he exclaimed, growing angry.
“But at the time I thought you’d fully guessed,” Smerdyakov countered with a perfectly innocent air.
“Had I guessed, I’d have stayed,” cried Ivan.
“Well, I took it that you’d guessed, and that’s why you left in such a rush, just to get clear of the trouble, just to run away and save yourself in your fright.”
“You think everyone’s as big a coward as you are?”
“Forgive me, I thought you were the same as me.”

“Of course I should have guessed,” said Ivan, agitated, “and I did guess you were up to some mischief ... only you’re lying, you’re lying again,” he cried, remembering all at once. “Do you remember coming up to the carriage and saying to me, ‘It’s always worth while speaking to a clever man’? So you were glad I was leaving, since you complimented me?”
Smerdyakov kept sighing. A little color came into his face.

“If I was pleased,” he said, somewhat out of breath, “it was only because you’d agreed to go to Tchermashnya and not to Moscow. It was nearer, after all. But when I said those words, I didn’t mean them as praise but as a reproach. You didn’t understand.”
“What reproach?”
“That you saw such a calamity coming and still abandoned your own father, and wouldn’t protect us. I might have been arrested any day for stealing that three thousand.”
“Damn you!” Ivan swore again. “Wait a moment. Did you tell the prosecutor and the investigating lawyer about those knocks?”
“I told them everything exactly as it was.”
Once more Ivan marveled to himself.

“If I suspected anything then,” he began again, “it was only some wickedness on your part. Dmitri might kill him, but steal—I didn’t believe that then.... But I was ready for any wickedness from you. You told me yourself you could fake a fit. Why did you say that?”
“Out of plain simplicity. I’ve never faked a fit on purpose in my life. I only said it to boast to you. It was just foolish. I liked you so much then, and I was frank with you.”
“My brother flatly accuses you of the murder and the theft.”

“What else can he do?” said Smerdyakov with a bitter grin. “And who’ll believe him, with all the proofs against him? Grigory Vassilyevitch saw the door open. What can he say to that? But never mind him! He’s shaking with fear, trying to save himself.”
He trailed off slowly, then suddenly added, as if on second thought:

“And here’s something else. He wants to put it on me and make out I did it with my own hands—I’ve heard that already. But as for my being clever at faking a fit: would I have told you beforehand that I could fake one, if I really had planned something against your father? If I’d been planning such a murder, would I have been fool enough to give evidence against myself ahead of time? And to his own son! I swear! Is that likely? As if that could be—it’s never happened. Nobody hears this talk of ours now but Providence itself, and if you were to tell it to the prosecutor and Nikolay Parfenovitch, you’d be defending me completely, because who would be such a criminal if he’s so open-hearted beforehand? Anyone can see that.”

“Well,” said Ivan, rising to cut the talk short, struck by Smerdyakov’s last argument, “I don’t suspect you in the least, and in fact I think it’s absurd to suspect you. On the contrary, I’m grateful to you for putting my mind at ease. Now I’m going, but I’ll come again. Meanwhile, good-by. Get well. Do you need anything?”
“I’m very grateful for everything. Marfa Ignatyevna doesn’t forget me, and out of her kindness she gets me anything I need. Good people visit me every day.”
“Good-by. But I won’t say anything about your being able to fake a fit, and I advise you not to either,” something made Ivan say suddenly.
“I quite understand. And if you say nothing about that, I’ll say nothing about our conversation at the gate.”

So Ivan left. He had gone a dozen steps along the corridor when he felt all at once that Smerdyakov’s last words had an insulting meaning. He nearly turned back, but the urge passed, and muttering “Nonsense!” he walked out of the hospital.

His main feeling was relief that the murderer was Mitya and not Smerdyakov, though you would have expected the reverse. He did not want to analyze why, and in fact felt a real distaste for prying into his own feelings. He seemed to want to hurry up and forget something. Over the next few days he became convinced of Mitya’s guilt, as he learned how heavy the evidence against him was. Some of it came from unimportant people, Fenya and her mother for example, yet its effect was almost crushing. As for Perhotin, the people at the tavern and at Plotnikov’s shop, and the witnesses at Mokroe, their evidence looked conclusive. It was the details that did the damage. The secret of the knocks impressed the lawyers nearly as much as Grigory’s evidence about the open door. Grigory’s wife, Marfa, answering Ivan’s questions, declared that Smerdyakov had lain all night on the other side of the partition wall. “He was not three paces from our bed.” She was a sound sleeper, yet she had woken several times and heard him groaning. “He was groaning the whole time, groaning without a stop.”
Ivan told Herzenstube that in his opinion Smerdyakov was not mad, only rather weak, and drew nothing from the old man but a subtle smile.

“Do you know how he passes his time now?” he asked. “Memorizing lists of French words. He keeps an exercise book under his pillow, with the French words written out in Russian letters for him by someone, he he he!”

In the end Ivan put all his doubts aside. He could not think of Dmitri without disgust. One thing only was odd. Alyosha stuck to it that Dmitri was not the murderer and that “in all probability” Smerdyakov was. Ivan had always felt that Alyosha’s opinion counted for a great deal with him, and so he was astonished by it now. Another odd thing was that Alyosha never tried to talk to Ivan about Mitya, never raised the subject and only answered Ivan’s questions. This too struck Ivan in particular.

But at that time something quite different was taking up most of his mind. On his return from Moscow he had given himself up, hopelessly, to a mad and consuming passion for Katerina Ivanovna. This is not the place to begin on that new passion of Ivan’s, which left its mark on the whole rest of his life. It would make the subject of another novel, which I may never write. But I cannot leave out one thing here. When Ivan, as I’ve already related, left Katerina Ivanovna with Alyosha and told him, “I am not keen on her,” it was an absolute lie. He loved her madly, though at times he hated her so much that he could have murdered her. Many causes helped to produce this feeling. Shattered by what had happened with Mitya, on Ivan’s return she had rushed to meet him as her one salvation. She had been hurt, insulted and humiliated in her feelings. And now back to her had come the man who had loved her so ardently before (oh! she knew that very well), and whose heart and intellect she thought far superior to her own. But the sternly virtuous girl did not surrender altogether to the man she loved, in spite of the Karamazov violence of his passions and the great fascination he had for her. At the same time she was constantly tormented by remorse for having deserted Mitya, and in moments of discord and violent anger (and there were plenty) she told Ivan so plainly. This was what he had meant when he told Alyosha, “lies upon lies.” There was, of course, much that was false in it, and that angered Ivan more than anything.... But of all this later.

For a time he did, in fact, almost forget that Smerdyakov existed. And yet, two weeks after his first visit, the same strange thoughts as before began to haunt him. It is enough to say that he kept asking himself why, on that last night in Fyodor Pavlovitch’s house, he had crept out onto the stairs like a thief and listened for what his father was doing below. Why had he remembered that afterwards with disgust? Why had he been suddenly so depressed on the journey next morning? Why, when he reached Moscow, had he said to himself, “I am a scoundrel”? And now he almost thought these tormenting thoughts would make him forget even Katerina Ivanovna, so completely had they taken hold of him again. It was just after thinking this that he met Alyosha in the street. He stopped him at once and put a question to him:

“Do you remember when Dmitri burst in after dinner and beat father, and afterwards, out in the yard, I told you I kept ‘the right to desire’?... Tell me, did you think then that I desired father’s death, or not?”
“Yes, I thought so,” Alyosha answered softly.

“And it was true. There was no guessing about it. But didn’t you also suppose that what I wanted was just ‘one reptile devouring another’; that is, that Dmitri should kill father, and as soon as possible ... and that I myself was even ready to help it along?”
Alyosha went rather pale and looked silently into his brother’s face.
“Speak!” cried Ivan. “More than anything I want to know what you thought then. I want the truth, the truth!”
He drew a deep breath and glared at Alyosha before the answer came.
“Forgive me, I thought that too, at the time,” Alyosha whispered, and he did not add a single softening word.

“Thanks,” snapped Ivan, and he left Alyosha and hurried on his way. From then on Alyosha noticed that Ivan clearly avoided him and even seemed to have taken a dislike to him, so much so that Alyosha stopped going to see him. Immediately after that meeting Ivan did not go home but went straight back to Smerdyakov.
